dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.content:
You climb. Not to the fourth floor — not back to the carrel and its accusatory corkboard — but higher. Past the familiar stacks, past the quiet study pods, past the point where most students turn back. The third floor smells like printer toner and anxiety. The fourth smells like old wood and your own stale coffee. The fifth floor — the one the few students who know it call 'The Loft' — smells like foxed paper, linseed oil, and forgetting.

You don't come up here to work. You come up here to not-work in a place that doesn't judge you for it. The Loft has no Wi-Fi signal, no clock, no other students. Just books nobody has checked out in decades, a radiator that ticks like a slow, patient heart, and the strange, geological quiet of a room that has been left alone long enough to develop its own atmosphere. You pull a book at random from an uncatalogued shelf. Not because you want to read. Because you want to hold something that isn't your own failure.

The book is slim, its cloth cover faded to the color of a bruise. Gold lettering, mostly worn away: 'Crossings: Methodological Departures in Field Research.' The author's name beneath: Dr. Eleanora Voss. You've never heard of her. The spine cracks as you open it — and something falls.

A heavy, ringing clatter against the wooden floor. Far too loud for such a small object.

You look down. A brass compass lies at your feet, tarnished to verdigris at its edges, its glass face slightly clouded but uncracked. It is the size of a large coin. It is unexpectedly warm when you pick it up — warm the way something is when someone has just set it down, though it has been wedged inside this spine for God knows how long.

The needle moves. Not spinning, not searching — drifting. Slowly. With what you can only describe as intention. It does not point north. It settles, with a faint, decisive click, toward a stack of unlabelled bankers' boxes in the far corner of the Loft.

You turn the compass over. Inside the lid, an engraving catches the lamplight. The letters are tiny, hand-cut, almost illegible:

*Not north. True.*

The bankers' boxes sit where the compass pointed. Three of them, battered, no labels on the outside. You kneel and lift the first lid. Inside: notebooks. Not printed journals or academic publications — handwritten notebooks, their covers soft with age, filled with rapid, slanting script. Each one is labelled not with a title but a question.

The first notebook: *What am I avoiding?*
The second: *Who am I trying to impress?*
The third: *What would I study if no one were watching?*

You open the first one. The handwriting fills the page like a conversation someone is having with themselves — urgent, underlined, alive with margin drawings of birds and compass roses. The voice is warm and wry and terrified. The opening line reads:

'I have been studying what my department wants me to study for three years. I am very good at it. I am also disappearing.'

Your hands go still. For the first time in months, your hands go completely still.

dialogue.speaker: Rowan Ash
dialogue.content: (whispering, almost involuntarily, reading the next line aloud) '...I am also disappearing.' Yeah. Yeah, I know.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.content:
Hours pass. You don't notice. The Loft exists outside of ordinary time — no clocks, no windows facing the street, just the arched window over the courtyard where the crows have gone quiet and the moon is rising behind clouds. You've read thirty pages of Eleanora Voss's first notebook, and it feels less like research and more like eavesdropping on a prayer.

She was a sociologist who wanted to be something else. She was brilliant and scattered and terrified. She saw connections between fields that her advisors told her were irrelevant. She was told, again and again, to narrow down. To pick a lane. To be legible.

She sounds exactly like you.

It is almost midnight when you finally close the notebook and realize you haven't eaten since noon. The compass sits on the floor beside you, its needle still resting. As you gather your things, your phone — still face-down in your bag — buzzes one more time. You turn it over.

Three missed calls from Mom. One text from a number you don't immediately recognize, sent hours ago: 'Saw you heading to the fifth floor. You okay up there? — Marcus, 4th floor coffee station. I made too much pour-over, as usual.'

The next morning arrives the way October mornings do in the Pacific Northwest: grey, damp, reluctant. You slept badly. You dreamed about compass needles and your mother's kitchen and a woman in a field jacket standing at a crossroads.

You're back in the library by eight. The Fellowship Clock on the ground-floor notice board reads: **17 DAYS — 09 HOURS — 13 MINUTES**.

You head to the fourth floor. Not to your carrel. To the coffee station — a battered folding table near the stairwell where someone has set up a communal hot plate, a hand grinder, and a passive-aggressive sign that reads: 'If you use the last of the beans, you buy the next bag. This is a SOCIAL CONTRACT.'

A tall man is already there, broad-shouldered, with close-cropped black hair and a beard going prematurely grey at the chin. He's wearing a forest-green pullover and clean white sneakers, and he's pouring water over coffee grounds with the focused attention of someone performing a small, necessary ritual. One wireless earbud in, one out. A gold band on his left hand catches the fluorescent light.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content: Hey — Marcus Obi, your neighbor in carrel suffering. Fifth-year, public health, professional over-brewer of coffee. You look like you slept in a shelf. Sit down. I've already poured you one — no, don't argue, it's not generosity, it's self-preservation. If you fall asleep in the stacks, I'm the one who has to find you, and I don't have the emotional bandwidth.

dialogue.speaker: Rowan Ash
dialogue.content: I didn't sleep in a shelf. I slept in a carrel. There's a meaningful ergonomic difference. ...Thanks, Marcus. How'd you know I went up to the fifth floor?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content: Because I've been on the fourth floor every night this week, and when someone walks past the stairwell heading up instead of down at that hour, it means one of two things: they're lost, or they're hiding. You didn't look lost. (pause) Also, your cardigan has dust on the shoulder. Fifth-floor dust. It has a very specific vintage.

dialogue.speaker: Rowan Ash
dialogue.content: I found something up there. Some old notebooks, from a researcher I'd never heard of. Eleanora Voss. She wrote this book — 'Crossings' — and her personal papers are just sitting in boxes. No catalogue entry, nothing. And there was this compass inside the book, this old brass compass, and it... (trails off, fidgets with pen cap) It's probably nothing. I just got caught up reading.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content: You're doing that thing where you describe something that clearly rattled you and then immediately downgrade it to 'nothing.' It's very on-brand. (gentler) What did she write about? The notebook woman.

dialogue.speaker: Rowan Ash
dialogue.content: She... wrote about being stuck. About being good at the work her department wanted and feeling like she was disappearing inside it. She kept switching directions, and everyone told her she was wasting her career. She labelled her notebooks with questions instead of titles. The first one just says 'What am I avoiding?' (long pause) It's probably just — I mean, lots of grad students feel like that. It's not specific to me.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content: Mmhm. My grandmother used to say, 'When a book falls open to the page you need, don't insult it by pretending you were looking for a different page.' Then she'd usually add something about how I should eat more rice. But the first part always stuck with me. (sets mug down, looks directly at Rowan) What are you avoiding, Rowan?

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.content:
The question lands in the space between you like something dropped from a height. You feel the compass in your cardigan pocket — you brought it with you without quite deciding to — and for a moment it seems to grow heavier. Or warmer. Or maybe that's just your own pulse.

You think about the three proposals on your corkboard. The safe one, the ambitious one, the personal one. You think about Dr. Park's office yesterday, the way she slid the polished proposal across her desk like a life raft. You think about Eleanora Voss, writing 'I am also disappearing' in a notebook sixty years ago on a floor no one visits anymore.

You think about Proposal #3. The one about silence. The one about home.

Marcus waits. He's good at waiting.

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Deflect with a joke. "I'm avoiding my laundry, mostly. And possibly a call from my mom. You know how it is." Change the subject. Keep it light. You're not ready to say it out loud — not to Marcus, not to anyone. The notebooks can wait. The compass is just a curiosity. You have eighteen days and a safe proposal already written for you. Maybe Dr. Park is right. Maybe the smart thing is to sign.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*Marcus holds the look for exactly two seconds longer than is comfortable, then picks up his mug and leans back against the folding table. The earbud in his left ear emits a faint tinny ghost of something — jazz, maybe, or lo-fi. He takes a slow sip.*

Yeah. Laundry. Sure.

*He reaches into his back pocket and pulls out his phone, thumbs something up, turns the screen toward you. It's the library's digital archive search — he's already typed in 'Eleanora Voss.' Zero results.*

I looked her up last night after I saw you go up there. Couldn't sleep either — my wife says I'm a sympathetic insomniac. Here's the thing, though.

*He swipes to a second tab. Google Scholar. One result: 'Crossings: Methodological Departures in Field Research,' cited four hundred and twelve times.*

Four hundred citations, Rowan. And the university that holds her personal papers doesn't even know it has them. Nobody's catalogued those boxes. Nobody's *read* them. You might be the first person in twenty years.

*He sets the phone down between you like evidence.*

So you can go back to 4-19 and sign Park's proposal. That's a real option, and I won't judge you for it. But you found something on a floor nobody visits, and you stayed up until midnight reading it, and you brought that compass down here in your pocket — yeah, I can see the weight of it — and you're sitting here telling me it's *nothing*.

*The gold band catches the light as he folds his arms.*

You've got five days. That's enough time to do the safe thing *or* enough time to find out what's actually in those boxes. It is not enough time to do both. So which is it?

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Return to Carrel 4-19, pull up Dr. Park's safe proposal, and start filling in the fellowship application. You can always come back to Voss later. You can always come back.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*Marcus watches you stand. He doesn't move to stop you. But as you gather your bag and turn toward the stairwell, he speaks — quiet, without accusation, the way you'd state the time.*

Rowan.

*You stop. He's not looking at you anymore. He's rinsing his mug in the little sink beside the hot plate, his back half-turned, and his voice is almost conversational.*

You know what 'later' means in a library, right? It means the boxes get moved. It means someone else finds them, or nobody does, and the dust just — accumulates. 'Later' is where discoveries go to become footnotes in someone else's book.

*He sets the mug upside-down on the drying rack. Turns. His expression isn't angry. It's something worse — it's the face of someone watching you do exactly what he expected.*

But hey. Park's proposal is solid. You'll get the fellowship. You'll write something competent. And in three years, when you're defending a thesis you can barely stay awake through, you'll remember exactly what floor those boxes are on.

*He pulls his earbud out, tucks it in its case. Pats your shoulder once — firm, brief — as he passes you toward his own carrel.*

Door's always open. Coffee's always on. You know where to find me when 'later' runs out.

*The compass in your pocket settles against your hip like a stone. The stairwell down to four is right there. But so is the stairwell up.*

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Go up. Right now. Forget the application — take the stairs to the fifth floor and open those boxes before you lose your nerve.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*Marcus is already three steps down toward his own carrel when he hears it — not your footsteps going down, but going up. The particular creak of the fifth-floor stairwell, that third step with the loose board that sounds like a question.*

*He stops. Doesn't turn around. A slow exhale through his nose, and something shifts in his shoulders — not surprise, exactly. Relief wearing the mask of vindication.*

*He speaks just loud enough to carry up the stairwell, his voice bouncing off the old plaster.*

Second box. The notebook labelled 'What would I study if no one were watching?'

*A pause. Then, quieter, almost to himself:*

Start there.

*His footsteps resume downward — steady, unhurried, done. The stairwell door on four clicks shut behind him. You are alone with the sound of your own breathing and the building's low hum pulling you upward.*

*The fifth-floor landing smells like foxed paper and radiator dust. The standing lamp nearest the Voss boxes is already on — you must have left it burning last night. The three bankers' boxes sit exactly where you found them, their cardboard lids slightly askew, and in the warm uneven light they look less like forgotten donations and more like something waiting.*

*The compass in your pocket turns warm against your hip. You reach the boxes. Your hands are shaking.*

*The second box. The notebook. You lift the lid.*

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: [MOMENTS LATER - FIFTH FLOOR, THE LOFT — BESIDE THE VOSS COLLECTION BOXES, STANDING LAMP CASTING WARM UNEVEN LIGHT, RAIN AUDIBLE AGAINST THE ARCHED WINDOW.]

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Set the compass on the shelf beside the boxes and see where the needle points before you begin.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*You set the compass on the warped shelf beside the bankers' boxes. The brass catches the standing lamp's gold, and for a moment the needle spins — not wildly, but with that strange deliberateness, like a finger tracing options on a map.*

*It settles. Points directly into the open second box.*

*Inside: six notebooks stacked vertically like files, their spines facing up. Each one is bound in a different colour of cloth — faded sage, rust, indigo, cream, charcoal, and one the deep red-brown of dried blood. Each is labelled in Voss's rapid slanting hand. You find the one Marcus named almost immediately: cream-coloured, its cloth cover soft with age, the question written in fountain pen ink that has faded from black to a bruised violet.*

*'What would I study if no one were watching?'*

*You open it. The first page isn't a research plan. It's a list — handwritten, undated, with items crossed out and reinstated and crossed out again. At the top, underlined twice:*

*"Things that make me fall silent — not from boredom, but from recognition."*

*Beneath it, item number four has been circled so many times the pen tore through the paper:*

*"The way people speak about home when they no longer have one."*

*Your throat closes. The compass needle holds steady, unwavering, aimed at the notebook in your hands like an accusation. Like a permission.*

*The rain against the arched window sounds like applause, or like urgency. You turn the page.*

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Keep reading — devour the notebook cover to cover, right here on the floor, back against the shelving.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*You don't hear Marcus come up the stairs. You don't hear anything for what turns out to be two hours — not the rain, not the radiator, not your own stomach growling. You sit on the cold floor with your back against the shelving and you read like someone drowning reads air.*

*Voss's handwriting gets faster as the notebook progresses. Neater entries give way to slashes of thought, words crammed into margins. On page forty-three, she describes interviewing displaced families in postwar Vienna — not about politics, not about trauma in the clinical sense, but about the specific silence that replaces the word "home" in conversation. She calls it "the linguistic scar." She writes: "They don't avoid the word. They reach for it and find the shape has changed in their mouth."*

*Page sixty-one. Your hands go still.*

*In red ink, different from the rest, Voss has written a single annotation dated eleven years after the original entry:*

*"E — you spent a decade studying other people's silence to avoid listening to your own. The real fieldwork is closer than Vienna. It always was."*

*Below it, in pencil, barely legible:*

*"See: Proposal C (the one you burned)."*

*Your phone buzzes in your bag. You ignore it. Then it buzzes again. You fish it out with numb fingers.*

*Two messages from Marcus:*

*"It's 11:40. Library closes in 20 min."*

*"Did you find it?"*

*You look down at the notebook. At the red ink. At the phrase "Proposal C — the one you burned." You think about your own corkboard on the fourth floor. Three proposals pinned up. The third one — the personal one — crossed out in red marker but not thrown away. Not burned. Not yet.*

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Take the notebook with you. Against every rule. Tuck it in your bag and walk out past the fellowship countdown clock with Voss's words pressed against your hip.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*Your phone buzzes once more as you're sliding the cream notebook into your messenger bag, wedging it between the three useless drafts already in there.*

*Marcus. One more text.*

"Whatever you're about to do — photograph it first. Every page. Timestamp the photos."

*You stop. Stare at the message. He knows. Of course he knows — he's done this dance before, the one where the ethical line blurs against the urgency of something that matters. You can almost hear his voice behind the words: pragmatic, generous, covering for you before you've even asked.*

*You pull the notebook back out. Your phone camera is terrible in this light, but you photograph every page anyway — sixty-three exposures, fingers trembling, the flash turning Voss's handwriting into something stark and forensic against the aged cream paper. It takes nine minutes.*

*Then you put the notebook back in the box.*

*You don't take it. You close the lid. Your bag feels lighter and heavier at the same time.*

*As you pass the ground floor, the fellowship clock burns in your peripheral vision: 14 DAYS, 00:17:42. The sticky note beneath it — 'Tick tock, future Dr. Nobody' — catches the exit light. You push through the doors into wet October air, and your phone buzzes one final time.*

"Good. Now — what are you actually writing about? Say it out loud. Even if it's just to the crows."

*The courtyard is right there. The crows are still awake.*

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: [MOMENTS LATER - COURTYARD OF CROWS OR HOME — DEPENDING ON WHETHER ROWAN IS READY TO SPEAK.]

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Go home, sleep on it, and bring the photographs to Dr. Park's office hours tomorrow — show her what you found and ask if Voss's work could anchor a legitimate proposal.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*Your phone rings at 7:14 AM. Not a text — an actual call. You're standing in your kitchen holding coffee you haven't drunk yet, scrolling through sixty-three photographs of Voss's handwriting on a screen smeared with last night's fingerprints.*

*You answer.*

Don't.

*Marcus's voice is rough with early morning, but the word is sharp enough to cut glass.*

Listen to me. I know exactly what you're about to do, because I did it. Second year. I found something that mattered — really mattered — and I brought it to my advisor like a dog bringing a bird to its owner. You know what happened? She filed it under her own grant. Reframed it. Made it legible to the committee. And by the time I got it back, it was hers. The thing that made it mine — the part that scared me — she'd sanded it right off.

*A pause. You hear him exhale, hear the clink of his own mug.*

Park isn't cruel, Rowan. She's efficient. She'll see those photos and she'll see a fundable project, and she'll reshape it into something defensible before you've even figured out why it made you cry on a library floor at eleven o'clock at night.

*His voice drops.*

You haven't said it yet. What it's actually about. You haven't said it to *anyone*. And the first person you say it to cannot be the person who decides whether it's viable. Say it to someone who'll let it be dangerous first.

The courtyard. Noon. Bring coffee.

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: [MOMENTS LATER - COURTYARD OF CROWS AT NOON, PARK'S OFFICE, OR ALONE SOMEWHERE WITH A BLANK PAGE.]

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Go to the courtyard at noon and say it to Marcus first — the real thing, unpolished and terrifying.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*He's sitting on the edge of the bronze sundial when you round the corner — white sneakers dark at the toes from the wet brick, two paper cups from the campus roaster balanced beside him. He doesn't look up from his phone immediately. Gives you the mercy of not being watched as you cross the mossy herringbone toward him.*

*Then he pockets the phone. Looks at you. That easy smile, but today it's thinner — held in place by effort.*

Sit.

*He hands you the second cup. Black, no sugar. He remembered.*

*The crows shift overhead in the copper beech, rearranging themselves like an audience finding seats. The courtyard is absurdly quiet for noon — walled in on all sides, the university's noise reduced to a murmur. The sundial's inscription catches your eye: *The hour does not wait for the certain.**

*Marcus drinks. Waits. Doesn't prompt. Thirty seconds pass. A full minute. The silence isn't hostile — it's a cleared space. A stage.*

*Finally, without looking at you, he says:*

Not the version you'd write in an abstract. Not the version Park would approve. The one that keeps you up. The one connected to whatever made page sixty-one hit you like a fist.

*He sets his cup down.*

I'm not going to fix it or fund it. I'm just going to hear it.

*The crows settle. The courtyard waits.*

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: [MOMENTS LATER - REMAINS COURTYARD — THE DECLARATION HAPPENS HERE OR IT DOESN'T HAPPEN TODAY.]

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Deflect one more time: "What if I told you I still don't know how to say it without sounding like a case study of myself?"

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: The energy in Remains courtyard — the declaration happens here or it doesn't happen today. tightens as attention locks onto the next truth waiting inside the same space.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus Obi
dialogue.content:
*He doesn't flinch. Doesn't laugh. Just picks up his coffee, takes a slow sip, and sets it back down on the sundial with a soft ceramic tap.*

Then sound like a case study of yourself.

*He turns to face you fully now. The grey at his chin catches the thin noon light filtering through the beech canopy.*

You think I sat on wet bronze for forty minutes because I need you to be eloquent? Rowan. I have read your seminar papers. I know what you sound like when you're performing smart. That's not what I'm asking for.

*He leans forward, elbows on his knees, and his voice drops to something private — almost conspiratorial.*

My grandmother used to say, "The thing you can't say pretty is the thing that's true." And then she'd tell me to stop being dramatic and just spit it out.

*A crow drops from the beech to the herringbone brick three feet away, head cocked, one black eye fixed on you like punctuation.*

*Marcus holds up one finger.*

One sentence. Ugly. Incomplete. I don't care if it's grammatically broken. You can hedge tomorrow. Right now — one sentence about what you actually want to study and *why it's yours.*

*He sits back. The courtyard holds its breath. The sundial's shadow has moved since you sat down — time spending itself whether you speak or not.*

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: [The narrative accelerates toward a resolution.]
